title: Binary Search
summary: Find `target` in a sorted array in O(log n). Look at the middle of the window `[lo, hi]`; if it's too small, the target can only be to the right, otherwise to the left. Each step halves the window.

complexity.note: Best case when the first middle is the target.

intuition: Invariant: if the target exists, it's inside `[lo, hi]`.
`mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` avoids int overflow.
Move `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`; `mid` itself is already ruled out.
The loop ends when `lo > hi`: the window is empty.

title: Search Insert Position
summary: Return the index of `target`, or where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. That's the first index whose value is ≥ target (the lower bound). Binary search with a half-open window `[lo, hi)` finds it directly.
intuition: Answer = first index i with `nums[i] >= target`; it can be n (insert at the end).
If `nums[mid] < target`, the answer is right of mid: `lo = mid + 1`.
Otherwise mid might be the answer: `hi = mid`.
When `lo == hi`, that's the answer.
pitfalls: Starting with `hi = n - 1` can't return n for targets larger than everything.
Mixing closed and half-open window rules.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
summary: A sorted array was rotated, e.g. [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]. Compare the middle with the rightmost element: if `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the drop (and the minimum) is to the right of mid; otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left.

complexity.note: Values are distinct, so every comparison discards half.

intuition: The minimum is the only element smaller than its predecessor: the rotation point.
`nums[mid] > nums[hi]` means the rotation point is in `(mid, hi]`.
Otherwise `[mid, hi]` is sorted, so the minimum is in `[lo, mid]`.
Stop when `lo == hi`.
pitfalls: Comparing with `nums[lo]` instead of `nums[hi]` breaks on arrays that aren't rotated.
Using `hi = mid - 1` in the else branch can skip the minimum.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
summary: Each row is sorted and starts after the previous row ends, so the whole matrix is one sorted list read row by row. Binary search over indices 0..m·n−1 and convert each index to `(i / n, i % n)`.

complexity.note: One binary search over all cells.

intuition: Treat the matrix as a sorted 1D array of length m·n.
Index k maps to row `k / n`, column `k % n`.
Then it's plain binary search.
pitfalls: Two separate binary searches (row, then column) also work but are easier to get wrong.
Using m instead of n (the number of columns) in the index conversion.

Python.code:
def searchMatrix(matrix: List[List[int]], target: int) -> bool:
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    lo, hi = 0, m * n - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        val = matrix[mid // n][mid % n]
        if val == target:
            return True
        if val < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return False

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
summary: Find `target` in a rotated sorted array in O(log n). At least one half around `mid` is always sorted. Check whether the target lies inside that sorted half; if so, search there, otherwise search the other half.
intuition: If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`, the left half `[lo, mid]` is sorted; otherwise the right half is.
For the sorted half you can test `target` against its two ends.
If the target is inside that range, keep that half; otherwise keep the other.
pitfalls: Using `<` instead of `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` breaks when lo == mid.
Getting the inclusive/exclusive bounds wrong in the range checks.
Finding the pivot first and then searching works, but is two passes.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
summary: Find the smallest eating speed k so Koko finishes all piles within h hours. Higher speeds only make it easier, so the feasible speeds form a range [answer, max]. Binary search k between 1 and the largest pile, checking total hours each time.

complexity.note: m = largest pile. Each check is one pass over the piles.

intuition: Hours at speed k: sum of `ceil(pile / k)`.
Feasibility is monotonic: if k works, k + 1 works too.
Binary search for the first k that works.
`(p + k - 1) / k` is an integer ceiling.
pitfalls: Summing hours in an int can overflow for large inputs; use long.
Upper bound must be max(piles); any faster gives the same hours.
Using float division for the ceiling.

Python.code:
def minEatingSpeed(piles: List[int], h: int) -> int:
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        k = (lo + hi) // 2
        hours = sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles)
        if hours <= h: hi = k
        else: lo = k + 1
    return lo

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
summary: Find the smallest ship capacity that ships all packages, in order, within `days`. The answer lies between the heaviest package and the total weight. For a candidate capacity, greedily fill each day; binary search the smallest capacity that needs ≤ days.

complexity.note: S = sum of weights. Each check is a greedy pass.

intuition: Lower bound is `max(weights)`: the heaviest package must fit.
Upper bound is `sum(weights)`: everything in one day.
Greedy check: load packages until the next one won't fit, then start a new day.
Bigger capacity never needs more days, so binary search applies.
pitfalls: Starting `lo` at 1 lets capacities smaller than one package "work" in the check.
Reordering packages; they must ship in the given order.
